doc.title: Marty Napoleon interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York, New York, January 16, 1999

title: The Napoleon Brothers piano quartet and the Sands Hotel booking
summary: Marty and Teddy formed a two-piano group, were booked via Jack Entrada, and clashed with the pit boss in the lounge.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: You had a quartet with your brother?

Oh yea, the Napoleon Brothers. That was great because we used to go to my mother’s house and we’d fool around at the piano, and my sister used to say, “why don’t you guys get a thing.” So we seriously thought about it. We had the first rehearsal at my mother’s house and man we worked well together. Because we’re both piano players, we’re brothers, but we never played together. So we played some things together, it sounded pretty good. So we said let’s get a group, and we started rehearsing and rehearsing. Meanwhile I had played the Sands Hotel with Louis’ band. And the manager was Jack Entrada, who used to run the Copacabana in New York. And Jack liked me. I hate to say it but every time I did a piano solo, I’d get a fantastic reaction see. So he used to come to me, put his arm around me, walk across the casino, he was a big guy, 6’3”, he put his arm around me he’d say “Marty, if you ever get a group, call me, I want you to call me, you’re welcome here anytime.” In fact I think one of his letters is in here. And he said anytime. So when Teddy and I started to rehearse, I went to Joe Glaser and he said, “well it’s hard to book two pianos, there are not too many jazz clubs which are going to get pianos” which is true. In fact we went into the Embers and we had, no was it the Embers? and we had a grand piano and an upright because it was hard to get two grands in a little jazz club. So Glaser kind of like dropped it, and I said well look, I’ve got a friend of mine named George Drake, he works with Bill Burham’s office. So I called and he says, “we’ll come and hear you.” So he came to hear us rehearse at Nola Studios. He says, “man you guys are great.” We got a bass and a drum, Georgie Shaw and Herbie Wasson. And the group sounded fantastic. So we’d been rehearsing for some time too. And I suggested I said look Jack Entrada has always said to me if you ever get a group, I’m going to call Jack. So they called Jack. He said, “send him out.” Just like that. He didn’t want to hear the group. He said, “send him out.” So they booked four weeks, with four two week options. Right? And we went out there and they loved us there, but we were playing in the lounge, and in those days the lounge was open. See nowadays I think the lounges are closed, and you have to go specifically into the room to catch the show. So you either © Fillius Jazz Archive -35-

play the big room or the lounge. And we were playing in the lounge and it was open. So now we’re playing on the stand and the bar was long, we were playing over here and the bar went long that way see? So actually we were playing out towards the audience this way and the people are gambling there. So what happened was, we were swinging so hard, that the people started turning around looking at the group and keeping time with their chips, and the dealers were getting bugged. They’d say hey man, you guys playing or what are you doing? So the pit boss would walk over to us one day and said, “hey guys, you want to keep it down please?” These guys were keeping time with the chips. So we said okay, so now we toned it down. Now we’re playing for the people in the bar. But the bar was narrow and long. So the manager comes over to us and says, “Hey, the people out there say they can’t hear you on the other end of the bar.” We said well the pit boss said — he said, “The pit boss said?” You’re working in the lounge, don’t listen to the pit boss, you listen to me, I’m the manager. So okay. So here comes the pit boss. “Hey you guys.” We said, “What? Speak to the manager?” He says, “Never mind the manager, we’re trying to make some money here.” It went that was for four weeks. And when we said, it’s never going to work, we’ll never pick up any options, we’re fighting with these guys. They’re going to throw us out pretty soon because they’re going to say hey, get lost. So after four weeks we split. Now we were the headliners. Napoleon Brothers, and in fact Barbara Carroll, she was on the bill, one of the things. And then we did three weeks like that and the fourth week we were working midnight to six AM. And my brother Andy was playing with a trio at another hotel, the Flamingo or someplace, the Sahara. And he was working from six to midnight. He’d finish work and he’d come over to see us. So now on the last week we said we’re going to try to leave here on closing night and get a good start, we had to go to Columbus, Ohio to play a gig there. So we said, “switch our schedule” so instead of midnight to six AM, they put us on from 6 PM to midnight. And you know what that did to us? It did this to our stomachs. It twisted us completely around, because we were going to be at 8:00 in the morning, getting up at 6, 5 at night, having breakfast and then going to work. It was crazy. Now all of a sudden we’re getting through at midnight, and started getting stomach pains. It was just crazy. So what happened was they gave our spot, that midnight to six, to Louis Jordan’s group.
